q: At his 1960 trial, what did Nazi war criminal Adolf Eichmann claim in his defence?
choices: He was just following his superiors' orders
He had never known what was happening to the Jews
He had acted in self-defence during wartime
He had been forced to sign a false confession
why: Eichmann said he was only obeying orders. The court found him guilty anyway, which sets up the lecture's question: inhuman monster, or ordinary man following orders?

q: What were the results of Stanley Milgram's 1961 obedience experiment at Yale?
choices: All participants gave at least 300 V, and 65% went to 450 V
Only a few obeyed, just as Milgram's colleagues had predicted
About 65% refused to go beyond 300 V once the student protested
Most stopped as soon as they heard the student bang on the wall
why: 100% gave at least 300 V and 65% went all the way to the 'life-threatening' 450 V. His colleagues had predicted only a few would obey, which is why the result was so shocking.

q: In the Milgram experiment, who was the real test subject?
choices: The volunteer who played the 'teacher'
The 'student' strapped to a chair in the next room
The experimenter wearing the lab coat
The colleagues who predicted the outcome
why: The experimenter and the 'student' were both actors, and the student never got real shocks (a tape recorder played the reactions). The volunteer 'teacher' was the one being tested for obedience.

q: Why was Milgram's experiment criticised, and why are its findings still taken seriously?
choices: It deceived people, yet replications found similar results
It used only paid actors, so its results could never be replicated by anyone
It paid volunteers too much, but the payments were later returned
Its shocks were real, but nobody was seriously injured
why: Critics called it unethical because it deceived people into what seemed like real violence. Yet it was replicated many times, with different populations, and gave similar findings.

q: What did Philip Zimbardo's 1971 Stanford Prison Experiment set out to explore?
choices: Whether a person's assigned role can change their behaviour
Whether punishment for wrong answers improves memory and learning
Whether prisoners can be rehabilitated through education
Whether students obey professors more readily than police
why: Zimbardo used a coin flip to make 24 screened students 'guards' or 'prisoners' to see if the role itself shapes behaviour. 'Memory and learning' was the cover story of Milgram's study, not Zimbardo's question.

q: The Stanford Prison Experiment was planned to last two weeks. What actually happened?
choices: It was shut down after only six days
It ran the full two weeks without any serious incidents
It was extended to a month because the results were so promising
It was cancelled on the first day when the Navy withdrew its grant
why: Guards abused their power within a day and several prisoners broke down. Zimbardo ended it on day six after his girlfriend, a former student, saw the conditions and confronted him.

q: Which later criticism led many to call the Stanford Prison Experiment 'a drama rather than an experiment'?
choices: Recordings show the guards were coached to act tough
Participants were screened to be mentally healthy
Roles were assigned to students by a coin flip
Each participant was paid $15 a day
why: Transcripts show Zimbardo's team told guards to be tough, prisoner 8612 later called it an improv exercise, and the prison consultant said the crueller treatments weren't the guards' own idea. Screening, the coin flip and the pay are just design details.

q: What general lesson does Lecture 1 draw from the Eichmann case and the Milgram and Stanford experiments?
choices: Many people will uncritically follow the commands of those in authority
Only people with violent personalities will obey orders to harm others
Ordinary people almost never harm others, even when an authority tells them to
Psychology experiments tell us nothing about real life
why: The slide says it directly: many people uncritically follow those in authority. That is the cost of lacking critical thinking, which the rest of the chapter addresses.

q: A new bank employee is told by her manager to backdate some loan documents. She feels it's wrong but does it, telling herself, 'It's not my responsibility, I'm only doing what I'm told.' What does this most closely mirror from Lecture 1?
choices: The uncritical obedience of Eichmann and Milgram's 'teachers'
Open-minded skepticism, Descartes' method of doubt
Collaborative learning that seeks a solution good for both sides
Perry's commitment stage, deciding on the best evidence
why: Like Eichmann and Milgram's volunteers, she hands moral responsibility to the person in power. The lecture asks exactly this: when a superior asked you to act against your standards, what did you do and how did you justify it?

q: According to Lecture 1, what can happen in everyday life to people who lack critical thinking skills?
choices: Bosses, family or friends may push their own agendas on them
They automatically reach Perry's commitment stage with age
They become immune to pressure from people in power
They start relying too much on reason and evidence
why: He warns that without critical thinking, others can persuade us into careers, universities or even marriages we later regret. Good critical thinking supports a better standard of living.

q: How does the textbook define critical thinking?
choices: A collection of everyday skills needed for full intellectual and personal development
The study of the methods and principles used to distinguish good arguments from poor ones
A belief based on careful personal feelings rather than on outside authority
The single skill of spotting and pointing out other people's mistakes
why: Critical thinking is a collection of everyday skills needed for full intellectual and personal development. The 'methods and principles' wording defines logic, which is only one part of it.

q: Critical thinking, according to the lecture, requires learning…
choices: how to think rather than what to think
what to think rather than how to think
which authorities to trust for the answers
to trust your feelings before the facts
why: The slide's phrase is 'how to think rather than what to think': it is about the process of reasoning, not adopting someone else's conclusions.

q: 'The study of the methods and principles used to distinguish correct or good arguments from poor arguments.' Which term is this?
choices: Logic
Critical thinking
Open-minded skepticism
Analysis
why: That's logic. Critical thinking is the broader collection of skills; logic is one part of it.

q: How does the lecture describe the relationship between logic and critical thinking?
choices: Logic is one part of critical thinking
They are two names for exactly the same thing
Critical thinking is one small branch of logic
Logic opposes critical thinking because it ignores feelings
why: Critical thinking, like logic, needs good analytical skills, and logic is a part of critical thinking. They are not synonyms.

q: In Lecture 1, an opinion is defined as…
choices: A belief based only on personal feelings, not reason or facts
A conclusion reached by weighing the reasons and facts on both sides
A belief shared by experts because it is backed by scientific facts
Any statement that can be shown to be either true or false
why: An opinion rests solely on personal feelings rather than reason or fact. That's what separates it from logic and critical thinking.

q: A classmate insists, 'Samarkand plov is better than Tashkent plov. I don't need reasons, I just feel it.' In the lecture's terms, this is…
choices: An opinion
A logical argument
An analysis at the third tier
Open-minded skepticism
why: He offers no reasons or facts, only a feeling, which is exactly the lecture's definition of an opinion.

q: Whose research on the cognitive development of college students is the source of the dualism, relativism and commitment stages?
choices: William Perry Jr., an education researcher
Stanley Milgram, a social psychologist
Philip Zimbardo, a Stanford professor
René Descartes, a French philosopher
why: William Perry Jr. studied college students' cognitive development; later researchers condensed his stages into three levels.

q: What is the order of Perry's stages of cognitive development, from least to most mature?
choices: Dualism → relativism → commitment
Relativism → dualism → commitment
Commitment → relativism → dualism
Dualism → commitment → relativism
why: Students start by deferring to authority (dualism), overcorrect into 'it's all opinion' (relativism), and mature into taking positions on evidence (commitment).

q: 'There are right and wrong answers, and authorities know the right answers.' Which of Perry's stages is this?
choices: Dualism
Relativism
Commitment
Confirmation bias
why: Dualists see everything as right/wrong or good/bad and look to professors, parents or politicians for the answer. Confirmation bias is a habit of this stage, not a stage itself.

q: Which of Perry's stages holds that when authorities don't have the right answers, everyone has a right to their opinion and there are no right or wrong answers?
choices: Relativism
Dualism
Commitment
Absolutism
why: Relativism rejects the dualist worldview and treats all truth as relative or a matter of opinion. Absolutism is a narrow-mindedness barrier, much closer to dualism.

q: What marks Perry's commitment stage?
choices: Deciding on the best evidence even though some uncertainty remains
Treating every opinion as equally valid, since there's no objective truth
Looking to professors, parents and politicians for the single right answer
Refusing to take any position until all uncertainty has been removed
why: At commitment you realise not all thinking is equally valid and authorities can be wrong, yet you still commit to positions based on reason and the best available evidence.

q: A first-year student says: 'Just tell me which answer is right. The professor knows it, so why should I think about it myself?' Which stage is she in?
choices: Dualism
Relativism
Commitment
Collaborative learning
why: She sees knowledge as something outside herself that an authority holds. That is the dualist stage.

q: In a seminar, Jasur says, 'That's just your opinion, and mine is equally true. Who are you to challenge it?' Yet he complains when the professor doesn't back his view. Which stage is this?
choices: Relativism
Dualism
Commitment
Open-minded skepticism
why: Relativists treat everything as opinion and look down on challenging others' views. The lecture points out the contradiction: they still expect the professor to support their opinion.

q: After reading studies for and against Tashkent's new paid-parking zones, Malika admits the evidence isn't perfect but concludes they will probably reduce congestion, and says she'd change her mind if new data appeared. Which stage is this?
choices: Commitment
Relativism
Dualism
Struggling
why: She accepts uncertainty but still takes a reasoned position on the best evidence, while staying open to revision. A relativist would say it's all opinion; a dualist would wait for an authority's answer.

q: Confirmation bias, which the lecture links to the dualistic stage, means…
choices: Seeking only evidence that backs your view, ignoring the rest
Changing your view every time somebody challenges it, to avoid conflict
Asking an authority figure to confirm which answer is the right one
Doubting every claim until it has been proven true
why: Confirmation bias is looking for research, facts and opinions that agree with you while dismissing the rest. Doubting claims until they are shown true is open-minded skepticism, which is a strength.

q: Before an election, Bekzod follows only Telegram channels that praise his favourite candidate and mutes any channel that reports criticism of him. What is this?
choices: Confirmation bias
Tolerance for ambiguity
Open-minded skepticism
Collaborative learning
why: He seeks only information that supports his view and shuts out whatever contradicts it.

q: Which of these is NOT one of the eight characteristics of a good critical thinker in Lecture 1?
choices: Absolutism
Open-minded skepticism
Collaborative learning
Flexibility and tolerance for ambiguity
why: Absolutism is a form of narrow-mindedness, a barrier. The eight are analytical skills, effective communication, research and inquiry, flexibility and tolerance for ambiguity, open-minded skepticism, creative problem solving, being attentive/mindful/curious, and collaborative learning.

q: Open-minded skepticism is also called the 'method of doubt', a term from René Descartes. What does it ask you to do with a claim?
choices: Not take it at face value, but require it to be shown true
Reject it, since most claims turn out to be false
Accept it if most people around you believe it
Ignore it unless it comes from an authority
why: The method of doubt means approaching a claim with an open mind but as a reflective skeptic, asking for it to be proven. It isn't automatic rejection.

q: A viral Instagram post says a herbal tea 'cures diabetes in 7 days'. Instead of sharing it, Dilshod comments: 'Interesting, but what evidence shows this works?' Which characteristic is he showing?
choices: Open-minded skepticism
Creative problem solving
Effective communication
Flexibility and tolerance for ambiguity
why: He neither swallows nor dismisses the claim; he asks for it to be shown true. That's the method of doubt.

q: Which characteristic means giving logical support for your beliefs instead of relying on opinion or experience, and evaluating others' arguments so faulty reasoning doesn't fool you?
choices: Analytical skills
Research and inquiry skills
Effective communication
Open-minded skepticism
why: That's the lecture's description of analytical skills, the first characteristic on the list.

q: A friend argues, 'My grandfather smoked every day and lived to 95, so smoking can't be that harmful.' Aziza explains why one case can't support such a general claim. Which characteristic is she using most directly?
choices: Analytical skills
Collaborative learning
Attentive, mindful and curious
Creative problem solving
why: She is evaluating the reasoning in someone else's argument so she isn't taken in by it, which is what analytical skills are for.

q: Which characteristic of a good critical thinker covers skills in writing, speaking and listening?
choices: Effective communication
Collaborative learning
Analytical skills
Attentive, mindful and curious
why: Effective communication. The professor skipped the details because students covered them in last year's communication course.

q: Before choosing a laptop for university, Sardor reads independent reviews, compares benchmark tests and checks warranty terms instead of buying the first one a seller recommends. Which characteristic is this?
choices: Research and inquiry skills
Open-minded skepticism
Creative problem solving
Flexibility and tolerance for ambiguity
why: He goes and finds the facts before concluding, which is research and inquiry. Skepticism is the attitude of doubting a claim; the stress here is on gathering information.

q: The lecture warns that 'too many people defer to others or fail to take a position on a controversial issue simply because they are unable to evaluate conflicting views.' Which characteristic answers this problem?
choices: Flexibility and tolerance for ambiguity
Effective communication
Collaborative learning
Creative problem solving
why: Sorting through conflicting claims takes discernment and tolerance for ambiguity: being patient and able to function when things aren't clear-cut.

q: Economists disagree about whether a new tax rule will help Uzbek IT startups. Instead of giving up or simply copying her professor's view, Nodira patiently works through the conflicting claims and is comfortable that the picture is still unclear. Which characteristic is this?
choices: Flexibility and tolerance for ambiguity
Collaborative learning
Effective communication
Attentive, mindful and curious
why: She copes with unclear, conflicting views without deferring to authority or refusing to engage. That's tolerance for ambiguity.

q: Viewing problems from multiple perspectives, imagining scenarios in advance, and welcoming risk and even failure as part of reaching a deeper understanding describes…
choices: Creative problem solving
Flexibility and tolerance for ambiguity
Attentive, mindful and curious
Research and inquiry skills
why: Creative thinkers come up with original solutions, foresee scenarios so they are better prepared, and treat failure as part of the process.

q: A student team's delivery app flops at launch. Instead of quitting, they treat the failure as information, sketch three new designs and imagine how users would react to each. Which characteristic is this?
choices: Creative problem solving
Analytical skills
Open-minded skepticism
Effective communication
why: Multiple perspectives, foreseeing scenarios and accepting failure as part of the process are the marks of creative problem solving.

q: In a heated group-chat argument, Kamola notices she is getting defensive and asks herself why this topic upsets her so much before replying. Which characteristic is she showing?
choices: Attentive, mindful and curious
Effective communication
Analytical skills
Creative problem solving
why: Critical thinkers are attentive and mindful not only of what's around them but of their own thoughts and feelings, and curious about them.

q: In Lecture 1, what does 'collaborative learning' mean as a trait of a critical thinker?
choices: Being open to others' views and seeking solutions good for both sides
Literally studying or doing homework together with classmates in a group
Letting the majority of the group decide so you don't have to think alone
Dividing up the research so that each member covers one part
why: He stresses it's not meant literally. Critical thinking happens in social situations, so you listen to others, anticipate their reactions, lower your own barriers and look for solutions that benefit both sides.

q: Two dorm roommates clash over quiet study hours versus having guests. Akbar listens to Sherzod's reasons, anticipates how he'll react, drops his own defensiveness and proposes a schedule that suits them both. Which characteristic is this?
choices: Collaborative learning
Effective communication
Flexibility and tolerance for ambiguity
Research and inquiry skills
why: Listening, anticipating reactions, lowering your barriers and finding a solution good for both sides is the lecture's collaborative learning. Communication skills help, but the defining feature is the two-sided problem solving.

q: What are the three levels of the textbook's three-tier model of thinking, in order?
choices: Experience → interpretation → analysis
Interpretation → experience → analysis
Experience → analysis → interpretation
Analysis → interpretation → experience
why: First something happens (experience), then you make sense of it (interpretation), then you raise the level and critically examine that interpretation (analysis).

q: 'You went to a job interview and were rejected.' At which level of the three-tier model is this?
choices: Experience
Interpretation
Analysis
Resistance
why: It's just the raw event or fact, with no explanation added yet, so it's the experience level.

q: A news report says fewer young people are voting. Your friend immediately says, 'That's because young people just aren't interested in politics.' At which level of the three-tier model is your friend?
choices: Interpretation
Experience
Analysis
Commitment
why: Your friend is making sense of the experience with a quick, simple reading that may rest on prejudice rather than information. Analysis would ask what's really behind it and what young people actually care about.

q: After his rejection, Timur asks himself: 'Was it really my lack of connections? Or my experience, or how I answered in the interview?' Which level of the three-tier model is this?
choices: Analysis
Interpretation
Experience
Struggling
why: He is questioning his first interpretation instead of settling for it. Analysis is driven by asking questions.

q: What does the analysis level of the three-tier model require?
choices: Asking questions to test your own and others' interpretations
Settling on the first simple explanation that makes sense of the event
Recording exactly what happened without adding any meaning to it
Adopting whichever interpretation an authority figure prefers
why: Analysis raises the level of thinking: you critically examine your interpretation and others', refusing readings that are too narrow or too broad.

q: In the textbook, 'resistance' as a barrier to critical thinking is defined as…
choices: The habitual use of immature defense mechanisms when our worldviews are challenged
Rigid beliefs that interfere with critical analysis of our worldviews
Holding two contradictory views at the same time and believing that both are true
Refusing to obey orders from superiors that go against our own moral standards
why: Because most of us dislike being proven wrong, we put up defences to protect cherished worldviews. The 'rigid beliefs' wording defines narrow-mindedness.

q: When does struggling with an issue stop being part of critical thinking and become resistance?
choices: When the struggle becomes an end in itself
When it takes longer than a single day
When you ask other people for their views
When you research the facts before deciding
why: Wrestling with an issue is a normal part of analysis. But when people get lost in details and what-ifs, achieve nothing and lose time, the struggle has become resistance.

q: Laziz must choose a capstone topic. For three weeks he keeps listing what-ifs and reading more about every option, misses the deadline, and still hasn't chosen. Which type of resistance is this?
choices: Struggling
Avoidance
Distractions
Denial
why: He is caught up in details and what-ifs and accomplishes nothing. The lecture notes that procrastinators are especially prone to this kind of struggling.

q: Lecture 1 praised a school director in Nepal who evacuated about 900 pupils minutes before a landslide. What point did this example make?
choices: He acted quickly on the facts instead of struggling
Decisions should wait until every uncertainty is resolved
In a crisis you should obey higher authorities without question
Collaborative learning means consulting everyone before acting
why: He saw the danger was serious and acted at once; ten more minutes might have been fatal. It's the counter-example to struggling as resistance.

q: Since starting university, Shohruh joins only chats and clubs where everyone shares his views, and skips any event where he might hear the other side. Which type of resistance is this?
choices: Avoidance
Conformity
Ignorance
Denial
why: Avoidance means staying away from people and situations that might challenge your worldview. Conformity would mean changing what you say to go along with a group.

q: When a classmate questions his claim during a discussion, Ravshan raises his voice, calls her stupid and refuses to continue. Which type of resistance is this?
choices: Anger
Denial
Clichés
Distractions
why: Meeting a challenge to your views with hostility shuts the discussion down instead of engaging with the reasons. That's anger used as a defense mechanism.

q: Whenever a hard moral question comes up, Zarina ends the discussion with 'Everything happens for a reason' or 'Things always work out in the end.' Which type of resistance is this?
choices: Clichés
Distractions
Denial
Ignorance
why: Stock phrases like these close a discussion without any real thinking about the issue. That's resorting to clichés.

q: Bobur has failed two midterms and games until 4 a.m. every night, yet insists, 'I don't have a gaming problem. I can stop whenever I want.' Which type of resistance is this?
choices: Denial
Distractions
Struggling
Avoidance
why: He refuses to admit a problem the evidence clearly shows. Distractions would mean using games to avoid thinking about some other issue; here the point is his insistence that there's no problem.

q: A friend offers Lola an article on working conditions in fast-fashion factories. She refuses to read anything on the topic so she never has to think about where her clothes come from. Which type of resistance is this?
choices: Ignorance
Anger
Conformity
Struggling
why: Deliberately refusing to learn more about an issue, on the idea that what you don't know can't hurt you, is ignorance used as a defense.

q: Everyone in Nilufar's friend group calls the new elective 'useless', so she says the same, even though she actually found it interesting, just to avoid standing out. Which barrier is this?
choices: Conformity
Avoidance
Clichés
Egocentrism
why: She goes along with the group instead of thinking for herself. That's conformity.

q: Whenever Akmal starts wondering whether his major is right for him, he opens TikTok or puts on a series so he doesn't have to face the question. Which type of resistance is this?
choices: Distractions
Struggling
Denial
Ignorance
why: He keeps himself busy with entertainment to avoid thinking about the issue. Struggling would mean getting lost in the details of the question itself.

q: Which of these is NOT one of the textbook's types of resistance?
choices: Egocentrism
Avoidance
Clichés
Distractions
why: Egocentrism is a form of narrow-mindedness. The types of resistance are avoidance, anger, clichés, denial, ignorance, conformity, struggling and distractions.

q: 'Rigid beliefs that interfere with critical analysis of our worldviews' defines which barrier?
choices: Narrow-mindedness
Resistance
Dualism
Cognitive dissonance
why: That's narrow-mindedness, which covers absolutism, fear of challenge, egocentrism, ethnocentrism and anthropocentrism. Resistance is the habitual use of immature defense mechanisms.

q: Absolutism, a type of narrow-mindedness, is the belief that…
choices: There are absolute right answers and certain authorities know them
The self is the centre of all things
Humans are the most significant beings in the universe
Every opinion is just as valid as any other
why: Absolutists believe in black-and-white answers held by authorities, much like Perry's dualist stage. The other choices describe egocentrism, anthropocentrism and relativism.

q: Whenever a teammate questions part of her code, Shahnoza feels personally attacked and worries that being wrong will make her look stupid, so she won't reconsider anything. Which barrier is this?
choices: Fear of challenge
Egocentrism
Absolutism
Conformity
why: She treats any challenge to her views as a threat and fears being wrong, which keeps her from re-examining her work.

q: Jamshid insists the group meet only at times that suit his gym schedule and judges every class discussion purely by how it affects him. Which narrow-mindedness barrier does this show?
choices: Egocentrism
Ethnocentrism
Absolutism
Fear of challenge
why: Egocentrism is the belief that the self is the centre of all things. Ethnocentrism is the same idea applied to your own group or culture.

q: A speaker tells foreign visitors, 'Our customs are the only civilised way to live; other nations' traditions are simply backward.' Which barrier is this?
choices: Ethnocentrism
Egocentrism
Absolutism
Clichés
why: Ethnocentrism is the belief in the inherent superiority of your own group or culture.

q: Someone argues, 'Animals can't really think or feel. They exist only to serve people, so how we treat them doesn't matter.' Which narrow-mindedness barrier does this show?
choices: Anthropocentrism
Ethnocentrism
Egocentrism
Denial
why: Anthropocentrism is the belief that humans are the central or most significant beings in the universe, which can blind us to what other animals are capable of.

q: After copying a classmate's homework, Ulugbek tells himself, 'The assignment was pointless, and everybody does it anyway, so it's fine.' Which barrier is this?
choices: Rationalization
Doublethink
Social dissonance
Ignorance
why: He invents self-serving reasons to justify what he has already done. That's rationalization.

q: Holding two contradictory views at the same time and believing both are true is called…
choices: Doublethink
Rationalization
Cognitive dissonance
Relativism
why: Doublethink (George Orwell's term) means holding contradictory beliefs without noticing the clash. Cognitive dissonance is the discomfort you feel when you do notice ideas conflicting.

q: The sense of disorientation you feel when new ideas directly conflict with your worldview is called…
choices: Cognitive dissonance
Social dissonance
Doublethink
Stress
why: Cognitive dissonance is the clash between new ideas and your existing worldview. Social dissonance is when other people's behaviour and norms clash with it.

q: A student from Tashkent starts an exchange semester abroad and feels disoriented because people's everyday social behaviour and norms clash with what she believes is proper. Which barrier is she experiencing?
choices: Social dissonance
Cognitive dissonance
Ethnocentrism
Conformity
why: Social dissonance is the disorientation you feel when others' social behaviour and norms conflict with your worldview. It would become ethnocentrism only if she judged their culture inferior to hers.

q: During finals week, exhausted and anxious, Asal stops weighing evidence and falls back on snap judgements and defensive habits she normally avoids. Which barrier is at work?
choices: Stress
Struggling
Distractions
Fear of challenge
why: Too much stress impairs higher-level thinking and pushes us back onto defense mechanisms and narrow-minded habits.

q: In logic and critical thinking, what does the word 'argument' mean?
choices: Using reason and evidence to support a claim or conclusion
A heated quarrel between people who disagree
Any statement of a strongly held personal opinion
A speech designed to win an audience over to your side
why: In logic, an argument isn't shouting; it's reasoning with evidence to support a conclusion. A speech built to win people over is closer to rhetoric.

q: Your upstairs neighbours are shouting at each other about who forgot to pay the electricity bill: no reasons, just accusations. In the logical sense, is this an argument?
choices: No, unless reasons are offered to support a claim
Yes, any disagreement between two people is an argument
Yes, raising your voice shows you are defending a conclusion
No, because an argument must be written down to count
why: In logic an argument means offering reasons and evidence for a claim. A quarrel made of accusations isn't one.

q: Why does Lecture 5 open with the 1858 Lincoln–Douglas debates?
choices: Their argument-then-rebuttal format is still used in debates today
Because Lincoln won the Illinois Senate seat by out-arguing Douglas
To show that emotional rhetoric always defeats careful argument
Because the debates overturned the Supreme Court's Dred Scott decision
why: One side presents an argument and the other answers with counter-arguments; scientific and political debates still use this format. Lincoln actually lost the election but became a nationally known speaker and critical thinker.

q: How did Lincoln change the national controversy over slavery in the debates?
choices: He recast it as a question of the whole nation's survival
He reframed it as a matter of each state minding its own business
He avoided slavery entirely and focused on the economy instead
He accepted the Dred Scott decision as the law of the land
why: Lincoln reworded the issue, which shows how the way you frame a question shapes the solution ('A house divided against itself cannot stand'). 'Mind its own business' and 'law of the land' were Douglas's positions.

q: In Chapter 6, what is an 'issue'?
choices: An ill-defined complex of problems involving controversy or uncertainty
A proposition in an argument that is supported by the other propositions
A statement about why or how something that already happened is the case
A position statement used to win people over
why: An issue is a messy, controversial problem that arguments help us analyse. The other choices describe a conclusion, an explanation and rhetoric.

q: According to the lecture, what goes wrong when an issue is not defined clearly?
choices: The discussion drifts and others can drag you off topic
The argument automatically becomes unsound and has to be dropped
You can then only use descriptive premises, never prescriptive ones
Nothing; clear definition only matters in written essays
why: A vague issue is a slippery path: you drift onto other topics, the other side can steer the discussion wherever it likes, and it can end in frustration. Defining the issue takes clear thinking and good communication skills.

q: You return to your dorm room and your wallet isn't on the dresser. Why does the lecture say 'Who stole my wallet?' is the wrong way to state the issue?
choices: It assumes, without grounds, that someone stole it
It is too neutral and open-ended to lead to any useful answer
It is a conditional statement rather than a genuine question
It focuses on the facts instead of on how you feel
why: All you know is that the wallet is missing; you may have misplaced it or it may be behind the dresser. The neutral issue is 'What happened to my wallet?', and open-mindedness is the trait of good critical thinkers and good detectives.

q: Your group project is behind schedule. Which is the best way to state the issue, following the lecture's advice?
choices: Why is our project behind schedule?
Why is Aziz so lazy that he's ruining our project?
Who is to blame for wrecking our grade?
How do we get an extension, since this isn't our fault?
why: The neutral question states only what you know. The others are loaded with unsupported assumptions about who is to blame.

q: Why does the lecture stress 'asking the right questions' when identifying an issue?
choices: Its wording shapes how we go looking for a solution
Asking questions lets you avoid ever committing to a conclusion
Asking enough questions guarantees that an argument is sound
It's only needed when you can talk to the other person face to face
why: The wording of the issue steers the search for answers. It matters even more with written material such as newspapers, where you can't clarify by talking to the author.

q: Which best matches the lecture's definition of rhetoric?
choices: Defending a set position to win people over, often ignoring opposing evidence
Using reason and evidence to explore an open question and discover the truth
Breaking an argument down into its separate premises and its conclusion
Restating an issue in neutral terms so that both sides can discuss it fairly
why: Rhetoric, the 'art of persuasion', defends a particular position, usually without adequate consideration of opposing evidence. Exploring an open question to find the truth is argument.

q: What is the key difference in purpose between rhetoric and argument?
choices: Rhetoric aims to persuade; argument aims to discover the truth
Rhetoric aims to discover the truth; argument aims to persuade
Both aim only to persuade, using different techniques
Rhetoric explains past events; argument predicts future ones
why: Straight from the slide: rhetoric → persuade, argumentation → discover the truth. Rhetoric also starts from a position already taken, while argument starts from an open question.

q: Why should a good arguer resist reducing an issue to two sides, with 'us' as good and 'them' as evil?
choices: Two-sided framing makes effective, creative solutions harder to find
Two sides are too few to keep a debate interesting for an audience
Polarizing an issue makes every premise automatically false
Arguments are only allowed to consider one side of an issue
why: Arguments should stay open to many perspectives. Framing an issue as a fight between two camps, which is common in politics, shuts out the in-between and creative options.

q: A candidate's campaign video lists only the benefits of his plan, calls his opponents 'enemies of progress', and never mentions any evidence against the plan. This is best described as…
choices: Rhetoric
An argument
An explanation
A conditional statement
why: It defends a fixed position, polarises the issue into good versus evil, and ignores opposing evidence, all in order to persuade.

q: A research centre hasn't taken a side on whether schools in Uzbekistan should move to a four-day week. It gathers evidence from several countries and invites feedback before reaching a view. This is closer to…
choices: Argument, because the aim is to discover the truth
Rhetoric, because it hopes to persuade the government
An explanation, because it describes other countries
Polarization, because it compares only two options
why: It starts from an open question, considers multiple perspectives and invites feedback, which is how the lecture describes argument.

q: Besides giving reasons, what should a good argument do, according to the lecture?
choices: Use language suited to its audience and invite feedback
Avoid feedback that might weaken its conclusion
Present the issue as having exactly two sides
Begin from a firmly held position statement
why: The purpose of argument is to present people with reasons, so identify your audience, pitch the language to them, and invite feedback and analysis.

q: How do the slides define an argument?
choices: Two or more propositions, one supported by the others
A single proposition that can be shown to be either true or false
A statement about why or how something is the case
An 'if… then…' statement linking two ideas
why: An argument is reasoning made of at least two propositions: the conclusion and the premise(s) that support it. The other choices describe a proposition, an explanation and a conditional statement.

q: What is a proposition?
choices: A statement that expresses a complete thought and can be true or false
A statement that has already been proven true by scientific evidence or observation
A question that opens up an issue for discussion
The main claim that an argument is trying to prove to its audience
why: A proposition only has to be capable of being true or false. 'Toronto is the capital of Canada' is false but is still a proposition. The main claim is the conclusion.

q: Which of these is a proposition?
choices: Toronto is the capital of Canada.
Is Toronto the capital of Canada?
Please look up the capital of Canada.
Let's visit Ottawa next summer!
why: It's a complete thought that can be true or false (here it's false). Questions, requests and suggestions are neither true nor false.

q: Which statement about an argument's conclusion is correct?
choices: It can appear anywhere, at the start as a thesis or at the end
It must always be the final sentence of the argument
It must always be introduced by the word 'therefore'
It is the proposition that gives a reason for another
why: The conclusion is what the argument tries to prove, and it can come first (as a thesis or topic statement) or last. Indicator words help, but they aren't required.

q: In Lecture 5, conclusions are also called…
choices: Claims, viewpoints or positions
Premises, reasons or grounds
Issues, problems or controversies
Explanations, causes or accounts
why: The conclusion is the claim, viewpoint or position being supported. Premises are the reasons for it.

q: What is a premise?
choices: A proposition that supports or gives reasons for accepting the conclusion
The proposition that the whole argument is trying to prove to be true
An ill-defined problem involving controversy
A statement about why or how something we already know happened came about
why: Reasoning runs from the premises to the conclusion. The proposition being proven is the conclusion itself.

q: According to the lecture, good premises are based on…
choices: Fact and experience, not opinion and assumption
The arguer's strongest feelings about the issue
Whatever the audience already happens to believe
Assumptions widely accepted in the culture
why: The more credible the premises, the better the argument. Culturally popular assumptions are exactly what the lecture tells you to check.

q: 'Canada has only one capital, and Ottawa is the capital of Canada. Therefore, Toronto isn't the capital of Canada.' What is the conclusion?
choices: Toronto isn't the capital of Canada
Ottawa is the capital of Canada
Canada has only one capital
Canada's capital is either Ottawa or Toronto
why: 'Therefore' flags the conclusion. The first two statements are the premises that support it.

q: 'Our university should keep the library open until midnight during exam weeks. Many students have no quiet place to study at home, and the dorm study rooms are always full.' What is the conclusion?
choices: The library should stay open until midnight during exam weeks
Many students have no quiet place to study at home
The dorm study rooms are always full
Exam weeks are stressful for students
why: Here the conclusion comes first, like a thesis, and the next two sentences give reasons for it. There are no indicator words, so ask what the speaker is trying to prove.

q: Descriptive premises are based on…
choices: Empirical facts from observation, science or the five senses
Value statements about what people should or shouldn't do
A comparison between two similar events or things
The definition of a key term that might otherwise be ambiguous
why: Descriptive premises report what is the case, based on observation or science. Value statements are prescriptive, comparisons are analogical, and definitions are definitional.

q: 'It's wrong to cheat on exams' and 'We should strive for diversity on university campuses' are examples of which type of premise?
choices: Prescriptive
Descriptive
Definitional
Analogical
why: Both are value statements about what's right or what we should do, which makes them prescriptive. They aren't empirical facts.

q: Plato said that just as a charioteer is in charge of his horses, reason should be in charge of our emotions and passions. Which type of premise is this?
choices: Analogical
Prescriptive
Descriptive
Definitional
why: It works by comparing two similar things (charioteer and horses, reason and passions). The word 'should' is tempting, but what makes it distinctive is the analogy.

q: When does the lecture say a definitional premise is especially important?
choices: When a key term is ambiguous or has several definitions
When the argument relies on scientific observation
When the arguer wants to compare two similar events
When the conclusion is a statement about values
why: If a key term like 'diversity' can mean different things, defining it keeps everyone arguing about the same thing.

q: A premise in a debate on public transport states: 'Passenger counts show that metro ridership rose after the new line opened.' Which type of premise is this?
choices: Descriptive
Prescriptive
Analogical
Definitional
why: It reports an observed, measurable fact, so it's descriptive.

q: In a debate about banning phones in class, a student offers the premise: 'Teachers ought to respect students' privacy.' Which type of premise is this?
choices: Prescriptive
Descriptive
Definitional
Analogical
why: 'Ought to' expresses a value judgement about how people should act, not an observed fact.

q: 'Just as a phone needs regular software updates to stay secure, a university curriculum needs regular revision to stay useful.' Which type of premise is this?
choices: Analogical
Descriptive
Prescriptive
Definitional
why: It supports its point by comparing two similar things, which makes it analogical.

q: Before arguing that plagiarism should be punished more strictly, Dilnoza says: 'By plagiarism I mean submitting any text, code or AI output as your own without giving credit.' Which type of premise is this?
choices: Definitional
Descriptive
Prescriptive
Analogical
why: She is pinning down the meaning of a key, possibly ambiguous term, so it's a definitional premise.

q: What is an explanation, and how does it differ from an argument?
choices: It says why or how something is the case; we already know it happened
It tries to prove that something happened by offering premises
It sets a condition with 'if… then…' but draws no conclusion
It defends a position without considering the opposing evidence
why: An argument tries to show that a claim is true. An explanation takes the event as known and tells you its cause or how it came about.

q: 'The cat yelled because I stepped on her tail.' What is this?
choices: An explanation
An argument
A conditional statement
A descriptive premise
why: We already know the cat yelled; the sentence just tells us why. 'Because' is the trap: here it introduces a cause, not a reason to believe a conclusion.

q: Which of these is an argument rather than an explanation?
choices: Bus fares went up and my stipend didn't, so I should cycle.
The bus was late this morning because of an accident on Amir Temur Avenue.
The baby cried because her mother left the room.
The exam was postponed because the professor fell ill.
why: It gives reasons (premises) to support a claim about what you should do. The others take a known event and explain its cause.

q: Why is a conditional statement like 'If you come from Russia, then you speak Russian' not an argument by itself?
choices: No claim or conclusion follows from it on its own
Because every conditional statement is false
Because it contains a premise indicator word
Because it explains why something happened
why: An 'if… then…' statement only links two ideas hypothetically. Nothing is actually asserted as true, so there's no conclusion.

q: 'If the national football team wins tonight, then the streets of Tashkent will be full of celebrating fans.' What is this?
choices: A conditional statement
An argument
An explanation
A descriptive premise
why: It has the 'if… then…' form and asserts no conclusion. It isn't an explanation either, since nothing has happened yet.

q: What order does the lecture give for breaking down an argument?
choices: Identify the propositions → identify the conclusion → identify the premises
Identify the premises → identify the propositions → identify the conclusion
Identify the conclusion → evaluate soundness → identify the propositions
State the issue → list the premises → establish the conclusion
why: First bracket the propositions, then find what the person is trying to prove, then find the reasons. The last choice mixes in the steps for constructing an argument.

q: In '[I think], therefore [I am]', what is the conclusion?
choices: I am
I think
There is no conclusion, only two premises
There is no premise, only two conclusions
why: 'Therefore' is a conclusion indicator, so what follows it, 'I am', is the conclusion; 'I think' is the premise.

q: Which of these is a conclusion indicator?
choices: Consequently
Because
Given that
In view of
why: Conclusion indicators include therefore, thus, hence, so, which shows that, for these reasons, consequently and it follows that. The other three introduce premises.

q: Which of these is a premise indicator?
choices: As shown by
Hence
It follows that
For these reasons
why: Premise indicators include because, since, for, given that, may be inferred from, the reason is that, as shown by and in view of. Careful: 'for' alone flags a premise, but 'for these reasons' flags a conclusion.

q: 'Students who sit in the front of a class generally earn higher grades. Therefore, you should move up to the front of the class, since I know you want to improve your GPA.' What is the conclusion?
choices: You should move up to the front of the class
Students who sit in the front generally earn higher grades
I know you want to improve your GPA
Students who want higher grades already sit in front
why: 'Therefore' flags the conclusion. The other two stated propositions are premises supporting it.

q: In the same front-of-class argument ('…Therefore, you should move up to the front of the class, since I know you want to improve your GPA'), what role does 'I know you want to improve your GPA' play?
choices: A premise, signalled by 'since'
The conclusion, signalled by 'since'
An explanation of why you sit at the back
An unstated premise
why: 'Since' is a premise indicator. A premise can come after the conclusion, so where it sits in the sentence doesn't decide its role.

q: 'We have to leave the party now, for the last metro train departs at midnight.' Which proposition is the premise?
choices: The last metro train departs at midnight
We have to leave the party now
The party will end at midnight
We might miss the last metro train
why: 'For' is a premise indicator here. The conclusion, 'we have to leave now', comes first in the sentence.

q: Which statement about breaking down arguments is true?
choices: It may fit in one sentence or several, with or without indicators
Every argument contains at least one premise or conclusion indicator
An argument must be spread over at least three separate sentences
The conclusion is always the first proposition you bracket
why: Arguments can appear in one sentence or several, and indicator words may or may not be there. Breaking them down helps you follow and visualise the line of thought.

q: Which list gives the lecture's five criteria for evaluating an argument?
choices: Clarity, credibility, relevance, completeness, soundness
Clarity, credibility, relevance, validity, cogency
Issue, premises, conclusion, organization, revision
Descriptive, prescriptive, analogical, definitional, explanatory
why: The five criteria are clarity, credibility, relevance, completeness and soundness. Validity and cogency weren't part of this lecture.

q: In a debate on 'Should social media be regulated?', you realise you and your opponent mean very different things by 'regulated'. Which criterion is at stake, and what should you do?
choices: Clarity: ask for clarification of the key term
Credibility: demand scientific evidence for every premise
Completeness: add the missing conclusion yourself
Soundness: declare your opponent's conclusion false
why: If a key term is ambiguous, ask for clarification. As the lecture puts it, 'know the battleground' before you fight on it.

q: When checking an argument's credibility, what does the lecture tell you to watch out for?
choices: Popular assumptions passed off as facts
Premises that are worded too clearly and simply
Conclusions placed at the start of the argument
Arguments that invite feedback from the audience
why: Examine each premise on its own and ask if it's backed by evidence. Be especially alert to assumptions that are widely accepted in a culture or put forward by someone who isn't an authority in the field.

q: A fitness influencer with no medical training argues: 'Everyone knows cold water after a meal causes stomach illness, so never drink it.' Which evaluation criterion is this argument most likely to fail?
choices: Credibility
Clarity
Completeness
Relevance
why: The premise is a popular assumption passed off as fact by a non-authority, with no evidence behind it. If it were true it would be relevant, so the weak point is credibility.

q: 'When my daughter was young, most doctors were men, so she should give up on becoming a doctor.' What does the lecture say is wrong with this?
choices: The premise is relevant but not sufficient to support the conclusion
The premise is completely irrelevant to medicine
The argument has no conclusion, only an explanation
The premise is a definitional one disguised as a fact
why: A premise can be relevant without giving enough grounds to accept the conclusion, and today many medical students are women.

q: 'Our football team has the best-looking uniforms in the league, so we'll definitely win the championship.' Which evaluation criterion does this argument clearly fail?
choices: Relevance
Clarity
Completeness
Credibility
why: The uniforms may really be the best-looking, and the claim is clear, but looks have nothing to do with winning. The premise doesn't support the conclusion.

q: 'Federal funding for education should be allocated by the size of a state. Therefore, Texas should get more federal money than Rhode Island.' What does the lecture use this example to show?
choices: Completeness: the premise 'Texas is bigger' is left unstated
Relevance: the premise is relevant but not sufficient on its own
Clarity: the word 'size' is too ambiguous to evaluate
Soundness: the conclusion has been shown to be false
why: The argument depends on the unstated premise that Texas is larger. Most Americans know that, but for an audience in Uzbekistan you might need to state it.

q: 'Scholarships go to the students with the highest GPA, so Shahzoda will get one.' What unstated premise does this argument rely on?
choices: Shahzoda has one of the highest GPAs
Scholarships are worth a lot of money
GPA is the fairest way to award scholarships
Most students would like a scholarship
why: Without 'Shahzoda has one of the highest GPAs', the conclusion doesn't follow. Spotting missing premises is the completeness check.

q: In the lecture, a sound argument is one in which…
choices: The premises are true and they support the conclusion
The conclusion is true, whatever the premises say
The premises are clearly worded, even if some are false
The arguer succeeds in persuading the audience
why: Soundness needs both: true premises, and a real connection between them and the conclusion based on reason rather than fallacious appeals.

q: If an argument's premises fail to support its conclusion, what can we say about the conclusion?
choices: Only that we don't know whether it is true or false
That it has been shown to be false
That it must still be true
That the argument is sound anyway
why: An unsupported conclusion is unproven, not disproven. The lecture's example is consciousness in other people, which probably can't be proved or disproved by logical argument.

q: Your friend argues that aliens have visited Earth, but his premises are weak and don't support his claim. You reply, 'So that proves aliens have never visited Earth.' What mistake are you making?
choices: Treating an unsupported conclusion as if it were proven false
Accepting a weak argument as if it were sound
Confusing an explanation with an argument
Leaving one of your own premises unstated
why: When the premises don't support a conclusion, the most you can say is that you don't know whether it's true. Weak support doesn't show it's false.

q: What is the first step in constructing an argument?
choices: State the issue clearly, in the form of a question
Establish your conclusion before anything else
Try your argument out on other people
Eliminate any weak or irrelevant premises
why: Clearly stating the issue, worded neutrally as a question, keeps you on track. The conclusion comes only after the premises are settled.

q: Which issue statement does the lecture give as properly neutral?
choices: Should the USA have stricter gun control laws?
Should the government do more to keep guns out of the hands of criminals?
Why do gun owners care more about guns than about public safety?
How can we stop the gun lobby from controlling American politics?
why: The neutral version doesn't build an answer into the question. 'Keep guns out of the hands of criminals' frames the issue so that one answer looks obvious.

q: You're preparing an argument about Tashkent's plan to cut down old trees to widen roads. Which issue statement best follows the lecture's advice?
choices: Should Tashkent widen roads where this means removing old trees?
Why is the city destroying our beautiful old trees?
How can we stop greedy developers from ruining Tashkent?
Should Tashkent finally fix its traffic by widening the roads?
why: Only the first is neutral. The others are loaded, either against the plan ('destroying', 'greedy') or for it ('finally fix').

q: When developing your list of premises, what does the lecture advise?
choices: Set your opinions aside and explore all sides of the issue
Choose only premises that support the view you already hold
Frame the issue as one right side and one wrong side
Write the conclusion first, then find premises that fit it
why: Stay objective, avoid the two-sides trap, brainstorm with others, use reliable sources, watch for unsupported assumptions and keep a skeptic's attitude.

q: While reviewing her list of premises, Madina wants to delete a well-sourced premise only because it goes against her own opinion. What does the lecture say?
choices: Resist that; drop only premises that are weak or irrelevant
Delete it, since premises should support your own view
Delete it, then add an opposite premise to balance things
Keep it, but move it into the conclusion instead
why: Step 3 is to eliminate weak or irrelevant premises while resisting the temptation to drop ones that don't mesh with your opinion.

q: When should you establish your conclusion, and what should it do?
choices: Only after settling the premises, taking in as many of them as possible
Before listing premises, so you know which ones to look for
After testing it on friends, picking whatever they liked best
At any point, as long as it matches your original opinion
why: You draw the conclusion only once you're satisfied with your premises, asking what follows from them and keeping an open mind.

q: If you present your argument as an essay, what does the lecture recommend for the opening?
choices: State the issue and your thesis early, ideally in one sentence
Hide the conclusion until the very end to build suspense
Leave the issue unstated so readers can work it out themselves
List every possible premise before you mention the issue at all
why: Put the issue in the first paragraph and the conclusion (the thesis statement) near the start, ideally as one sentence, plus a line or two on why the issue matters.

q: Once you've built what seems like a strong argument, you should try it out on others. What attitude does the lecture say to bring?
choices: Be open-minded and a good listener
Defend every point until the other person gives up
Present it only to people who already agree with you
Avoid feedback so that your confidence stays high
why: Testing your argument only helps if you listen. If it turns out weak, or the conclusion doesn't follow, you go back and revise.

q: During a practice debate, an opponent raises a counter-argument that Sanjar realises is compelling. According to the lecture, what should he do?
choices: Revise his position; refusing to would be irrational
Hold his ground, since changing his mind looks weak
Ignore it, because it wasn't on his list of premises
Switch to rhetoric to win the audience back
why: If a counter-argument is compelling, it would be irrational not to accept it and revise your position in its light.

q: Residents of a mahalla have built a strong argument that their street lighting needs fixing. Following the lecture's final step, what is the best way to act on it?
choices: Write to officials with a realistic solution and offer to help
Post angry complaints online until somebody notices
Keep the argument to themselves now that it's finished
Wait until every single resident agrees before acting
why: Good critical thinking has a behavioural component: where appropriate, put your conclusion into action, for example by suggesting a realistic solution and offering to help carry it out.

q: When constructing an argument, which step comes right after 'eliminate weak or irrelevant premises'?
choices: Establish a conclusion
Organize your argument
Develop a list of premises
Revise your argument
why: The order is: state the issue, develop premises, eliminate weak ones, establish a conclusion, organize, try it out on others, revise, act.
